title: Communicative English for Specific Purposes in Biology
reference: Course Plan, pp. 6–8; assessment tasks and marking criteria, pp. 9–13. Weeks 6–8 and 10–16 are grouped in the original plan. Their division into activities here is a suggested sequence. Week/day labels follow the supplied edition; confirm teaching dates for a new term.

weeks.topic: Course orientation and meeting your group
weeks.guide: 21 Nov. Explain the course aims, grading, pre-test arrangements, small groups, and how students sign up to meet a teaching assistant (TA). Demonstrate a short greeting.

slides.title: Meet your biology partner
body: Lecturer: “Hi, I’m Mali. I study biology. I like watching birds.”
Listener: “Which birds do you see near home?”

slides.title: Have your first conversation
body: Tell a partner your name and one biology interest.
Listen to their answer. Ask one question about something they said.

slides.title: Before you leave
body: Find your small group. Ask how to book your TA meeting.
Tell your lecturer one speaking skill you want to practise.

weeks.guide: 28 Nov. The syllabus specifies a pre-test in Google Forms. Use the form supplied by the course team and their instructions. The studio has no official test form or items.

slides.title: Before the course pre-test
body: Open the form your lecturer gives you. Check that you can hear any audio.
Tell the lecturer if you need help opening the form.

slides.title: After submitting
body: Write down one kind of English task you want to practise. Keep this note for the end of the course.

weeks.guide: 5 Dec. The course plan marks this week as a holiday.

weeks.topic: Group introductions and the picture vocabulary assignment
weeks.guide: 12 Dec. Start with the chapter 1 icebreaker. Explain the small-group plan and TA meetings. Introduce the picture vocabulary assignment from page 9. The syllabus lists 10 January as its submission deadline.

slides.title: Use a picture to start a story
body: Imagine a pond with a frog beside a water plant.
“A frog sits on a leaf at the edge of the pond. Then it jumps into the water.”

slides.title: Build your picture story
body: Choose one or two pictures. Use at least 20 words from the assigned biology list in a connected story.
Highlight each word you use. Check the meaning with a partner.

slides.title: Ask your listener
body: Read two connected sentences aloud. Your partner names the picture detail they heard.
Change one sentence if your partner could not picture it.

weeks.topic: Small-group listening and speaking with the TA
weeks.guide: 19 Dec. Run a short listen-and-repeat round, then rehearse a TA conversation. Use chapter 5 to extend clarification practice. The source schedules small groups and TA contact.

slides.title: Listen for the strong syllable
body: Your lecturer will say “microscope” twice. Listen, then say it.
MI-cro-scope. Put the strongest beat on the first part.

slides.title: Use the word in a question
body: A: “What did you look at under the microscope?”
B: “A leaf. I saw small cells.”
Ask your partner a new question about the leaf.

slides.title: Check what you heard
body: Say your partner’s answer back to them. If a word is unclear, ask “Could you say that word again?”

weeks.guide: 26 Dec. The syllabus groups weeks 6–8 together. This is a suggested order for two individual 2–3 minute talks and small-group listening practice. Give speakers time to share talk 1. Use the rubric on page 11.

slides.title: Build a short story
body: Beginning: “Last month I watched birds at the school pond.”
Middle: “One bird stood still. Then it caught a small fish.”
End: “Now I watch how birds move before they catch food.”

slides.title: Share your experience
body: Use a few key words. Tell the class your story for 2–3 minutes.
Listeners: write down the event and one detail.

slides.title: Check the order
body: Tell the speaker what happened first and what happened next. Ask about a detail you missed.

weeks.guide: 2 Jan. The syllabus groups weeks 6–8 together. This is a suggested order for two individual 2–3 minute talks and small-group listening practice. Invite students to share talk 2. Their interest can be personal or related to biology.

slides.title: Give a reason and an example
body: “I like watching ants because they work together. Last week I saw several ants carrying one piece of food.”
What is the interest? What example helps you understand it?

slides.title: Share your favourite topic
body: Speak for 2–3 minutes. Name your interest, give one reason and tell one short example.
Your partner listens for the reason and asks one follow-up question.

slides.title: Try one sentence again
body: Repeat your clearest sentence. Try a new example if the reason was hard to follow.

weeks.topic: Listen for details and finish your vocabulary story
weeks.guide: 9 Jan. The syllabus groups weeks 6–8 together. This is a suggested order for two individual 2–3 minute talks and small-group listening practice. Finish the two pre-midterm talks during the block. The course plan records the vocabulary submission deadline separately as 10 January.

slides.title: From a word to a sentence
body: “Root” names a part. “The root takes in water” tells the listener its job.
“The leaf is above the root” tells the listener where to look.

slides.title: Check your story with a partner
body: Read part of your picture story. Your partner points to each detail they hear.
Take turns. Replace one unclear word or add a missing detail.

slides.title: Before submission
body: Check that the story connects its events and highlights at least 20 words from the assigned list.
Follow the lecturer’s submission instructions.

weeks.guide: 16 Jan. The weekly plan marks no teaching in the midterm period. Confirm the calendar with the course team when reusing this syllabus.

weeks.topic: Choose an English biology story from the media
weeks.guide: 23 Jan. Weeks 10–16 share one syllabus block. This week is a suggested way to schedule its tasks. Ask each student to choose an English article or video to share and submit with their talk.

slides.title: Choose one idea from your source
body: Write the title and where you found the English article or video.
Find one image, event or fact you can explain in your own words.

slides.title: Practise a short opening
body: “I watched a video about a butterfly. It landed on a flower. I wondered what it took from the flower.”
Tell your partner which detail came from your source and what you wondered.

slides.title: Check the source
body: Show your partner the part of the article or video that supports your detail. Save your source for the lecturer.

weeks.guide: 30 Jan. Weeks 10–16 share one syllabus block. This week is a suggested way to schedule its tasks. Use this slot for the third 2–3 minute talk and the English source submission. Score the talk using the course rubric.

slides.title: Introduce the source
body: “My article is about frogs near a pond. One detail that interested me was their call.”
Use the title of your own source and a detail that is really in it.

slides.title: Give your talk
body: Speak for 2–3 minutes using key words. Explain the main idea and one detail in your own words.
Listeners: note one detail you could check in the source.

slides.title: Answer a listener
body: Ask: “What does that word mean?” or “Where did you see that detail?”
Speaker: answer in one clear sentence.

weeks.guide: 6 Feb. Weeks 10–16 share one syllabus block. This week is a suggested way to schedule its tasks. Use this slot for the fourth 2–3 minute talk. Have students bring the pictures and vocabulary story from their earlier assignment.

slides.title: Use your picture as a cue
body: “Near the tree, a beetle is on a leaf. Its legs hold the leaf as it moves.”
Which words tell you where to look? Which words tell you what happened?

slides.title: Tell the story aloud
body: Show your picture. Tell your vocabulary story in 2–3 minutes.
Speak from key words. Your listener chooses one biology word and explains it in context.

slides.title: Check for meaning
body: Ask: “Which part of the picture helped you understand that word?”
Listen to the answer and explain one word again if needed.

weeks.topic: Practise a conversation with the teaching assistant
weeks.guide: 13 Feb. Weeks 10–16 share one syllabus block. This week is a suggested way to schedule its tasks. Arrange the assessed TA contact according to the local booking system. The rubric separates attendance at a TA meeting from listening and speaking during the conversation.

slides.title: Clarify a question
body: TA: “Where did you find the insect?” Student: “Could you say that again, please?”
TA: “Where did you see it?” Student: “I saw it under a leaf.”

slides.title: Listen and ask back
body: A asks about a biology observation. B answers in a sentence.
A asks about one detail. B checks the question if needed. Swap roles.

slides.title: Check your reply
body: Did you answer the question your partner asked? Repeat the question in your own words before trying again.

weeks.guide: 20 Feb. Weeks 10–16 share one syllabus block. This week is a suggested way to schedule its tasks. Prepare the assessed group roleplay and explain how teamwork is evaluated. Students can choose a different biology situation.

slides.title: Choose a situation
body: Example: A class visits a school garden. One student describes an insect, another asks about its legs, and a third checks its location.
Decide what your group wants the audience to understand.

slides.title: Give every person a speaking role
body: Plan at least three spoken turns for each person. Use notes with key words.
Include one question, one careful answer and one request for clarification.

slides.title: Test the opening
body: Play the first minute. Ask a listener whose turn they heard and one fact they learned.

weeks.topic: Rehearse and improve the group conversation
weeks.guide: 27 Feb. Weeks 10–16 share one syllabus block. This week is a suggested way to schedule its tasks. Use the course performance criteria on pages 12–13. The roleplay duration criterion is at least ten minutes. Have each member practise a meaningful part.

slides.title: Listen for a useful reply
body: “I saw two insects near the tree.” “Where exactly?” “On the lower leaves.”
Which reply gives the listener new information?

slides.title: Run one rehearsal
body: Time your group. Follow the planned roles and speak from key words.
One observer notes a clear question and a point where the meaning was hard to follow.

slides.title: Make one change
body: Use the observer’s note. Try the unclear exchange again. Check that everyone has a speaking part.

weeks.guide: 6 Mar. Weeks 10–16 share one syllabus block. This week is a suggested way to schedule its tasks. One possible performance slot. Use the official roleplay rubric and the lecturer, self and peer teamwork criteria on pages 12–13.

slides.title: Perform the group roleplay
body: Speak to your partners and respond to what they say.
Use a gesture or point to a picture when it helps your listener.

slides.title: Listen to another group
body: Write down one question you heard and the speaker’s answer.
Share one example of clear communication.

slides.title: Reflect on teamwork
body: Use a specific example: “I helped our group by …” or “My partner helped when …”.
Complete the teamwork evaluation in the way your lecturer gives you.

weeks.guide: 17 Mar 2025 (B.E. 2568 in the source). Use the course team’s post-test in Google Forms. The source gives this date on page 8. The studio does not supply the official assessment items.

slides.title: Take the course post-test
body: Use the form and instructions your lecturer gives you. Submit your own answers.

slides.title: After the assessment
body: Read the speaking goal you wrote at the start.
Name one thing you can now do in English and one way to keep practising.
